doc.title: Mike Vax interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 29, 2022

title: Jazz education today: trophies versus history
summary: Vax criticizes contest focus and advises teaching jazz history.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: love of the music. It’s how many trophies do we have in the band room. And so they’ll rehearse three, four, five tunes over and over and over all semester so they can go and win trophies. And that’s not education. It’s not what Stan envisioned, it’s not what most of us in jazz education envision. And one of the things that when I do, sometimes I’ll do a clinic at a state convention for the educators. And I’ll say, “How many of you actually delve into the history of jazz music with your students? How many of you play old recordings for your students?” Rehearsals aren’t just about learning the tunes to go to contests. Rehearsals have to be part of making these students love the music. If you don’t know the history of the music how are you going to have a love for it? And so many young people, I mean it’s gone even farther now but a few years ago we were doing it young people would think that like Coltrane and Charlie Parker were like traditional jazz. They had no idea about what went on in the early part of the twentieth century in New Orleans and Chicago and San Francisco and New York and Kansas City. No idea. They barely know the name Louis Armstrong. You know? So what I tell the band directors is you know you’ve got the greatest thing to use right now and that’s the Internet. You know? You can go on YouTube and you can see people who died fifty years ago playing a concert. So on your — I can’t say blackboard anymore because the boards are all white now you know, say on your white board every week put a name. And your students have to google that name and they have to listen on YouTube and they have to go to Wikipedia and have them write a one paragraph thing about that person. And you know the band directors that have done it have said to me, you know, the students get a new — I don’t know maybe love of the music is wrong — but a new interest in the music because now they’re finding out where they came from. You know? I mean Gordon Goodwin writes wonderful charts but that’s not where big band music came from. And if all the band director does is mainly play Gordon Goodwin charts, and I’ve got nothing against Gordon at all, but why don’t they play some Basie charts? Why don’t they play some Kenton charts? Why don’t they play some Woody Herman charts? And if they were doing that at their concerts you’d be surprised how many of the parents and grandparents would say oh wait a minute, I remember that tune. You know? But I think that the education and the history has to be taught and it isn’t just about winning trophies.
